composition.operator_topic: Why our sourdough takes its time

first_pass_synthesis.full:
Sourdough is never really in a hurry, and neither are we.

The night before a bake day, I feed our two starters. Then the dough gets mixed in the afternoon and proofs overnight. By early morning, it’s ready to shape and bake in the deck oven.

Our country loaf is naturally leavened, with mostly bread flour and a little whole wheat in the mix. That long, steady rhythm is what we give it time for—before it goes into the oven for that dark, blistered crust.

You can find the country sourdough here every day we’re open.

corrective_pass_synthesis.full:
This is why our sourdough takes its time: it starts before the bakery is even open.

The afternoon before a bake day, we mix the dough. Then it rests and proofs overnight. Our starters are fed the night before, too—two active starters we keep in the walk-in fridge. They’re the beginning of every country loaf we make.

By early morning, the dough has had time to become what it needs to be. We shape it, bake it in the deck oven, and let the crust get dark and blistered. There isn’t a shortcut that gives you that same kind of loaf. Time is part of the ingredient list, even if it doesn’t fit on the label.

Our house country sourdough is naturally leavened, with mostly bread flour and about fifteen percent whole wheat in the mix. It’s the loaf I come back to again and again: sturdy enough for a sandwich, lovely beside dinner, and very hard to leave alone once it’s cut.

And then there are the breads that rotate through the week—the olive-and-rosemary loaf people ask about by name, the rye-caraway sandwich loaf that often disappears by mid-afternoon, and, when the weather turns cooler, our Friday dark-chocolate-and-sour-cherry sourdough.

But the country loaf is here every day we’re open. If you’re curious, come by and let us cut you a half loaf to take home.
